01  What the town knows — and what it doesn't

The record card is nine years out of date on the inside of your house.

Natick's FY2026 property record card for 24 Bishop Street was printed 14 October 2025. It is accurate about the things an assessor can see from a car, and silent about everything else — because the entrance log on that card shows the last time anyone from the assessor's office was inside this house was 25 July 2003. Since then: 2008 not at home, 2014 exterior only, 2022 exterior only.

That single line explains most of the gap between what the town thinks this property is and what it actually is — and it also explains the risk. Everything finished since 2003 exists in the house and not in the record.

Nothing here is a defect in the house. It is a defect in the paperwork — and paperwork is cheaper to fix than framing. But it has to be fixed before a buyer's inspector finds it, not after.
02  The land

Nearly an acre, and the town already discounts it by ten percent.

24 Bishop Street sits on 41,579 square feet — 0.9545 of an acre — which is roughly four times the typical lot in this comp set (median 10,363 sq ft). That sounds like a windfall. It mostly isn't, and the town's own valuation says so.

The land line on the record card carries an influence factor coded "Restr/Nonconfc" at −10%. It's a back lot: the house sits well off Bishop Street at the end of a long shared drive. The lot exists at that size because a back lot has to be that size — the acre is the price of admission, not surplus you can sell.

The cleanest proof is the parcel next door, carved out of the same 1995 split. It is a hair over half the size and the town values its land higher:

24 Bishop St · back lot$469,00041,579 sq ft  ·  −10% restricted/nonconforming  ·  $11.28 per sq ft of land
6 D St · street frontage$480,49023,553 sq ft  ·  no influence factor  ·  $20.40 per sq ft of land

Seventy-six percent more land, eleven thousand dollars less value. That is what access is worth, and it is already inside every number in this analysis — which is why you will not see me deduct for the driveway a second time later on.

What the acre does buy is real and should be marketed hard: a level, private-feeling rear yard with a paver patio and fire pit, mature trees on three sides, and no house directly behind you. In a submarket where the typical yard is a quarter acre, that is the property's best story.

The origin story, from the deed record: the land sold 1 October 1995 for $50,000 as part of a multi-parcel sale; the finished house transferred 28 June 1996 for $189,900. Same owners ever since — thirty years.

03  The market you're selling into

Natick is flat, fast, and unforgiving of a wrong price.

Every figure below comes from our own MLS PIN feed — 453 Natick single-family sales recorded since 21 March 2025, current through yesterday. Not an estimate service, not a portal. The actual closed record.

Median $ per square foot, by quarter

Five quarters, essentially one line. $464 in Q3 2025, $468 in Q3 2026 — up nine tenths of one percent in a year. There is no rising tide here to carry a stale listing.

How long homes actually take

Half of Natick sells inside 60 days. But 44 of 280 sat past 90 — and in this data those are almost uniformly the ones that opened too high. 23 Porter Road asked $899,900 in West Natick this spring, took 62 days, and closed at $820,000. An $80,000 lesson, two thirds of a mile from your driveway.

One house in the entire dataset sold twice — 3 Oxbow Road, in March 2025 and again in April 2026. Same house, same square footage, thirteen months apart: +2.4%. That is the cleanest read on Natick's direction anyone can give you, and it says the market is holding, not climbing.

05  The house next door

There is a near-identical twin sharing your driveway, and it has a paper trail.

22 Bishop Street came out of the same 1995 land split and the same 1996 build. The town's own record cards put the two houses side by side and they are almost interchangeable: identical ground floor area (864 sq ft), identical total living area (1,532 sq ft), identical full basement with two-car garage under, identical oil warm-air heat, identical Grade C / Average / 78% good, identical −10% land influence factor.

The differences are small and mostly favour you: your deck is 480 square feet against their 120, and you have a half bath they don't. They have one more recorded full bath and a slightly larger lot.

Its sale history is the closest thing to a price history your own house has:

One thing to know rather than fear: 22 Bishop is currently tenant-occupied. It was listed for rent in August 2025 and leased on 15 October 2025 at $4,165 a month against a $4,250 ask (MLS 73415674). A shared driveway with a rental is a thing buyers ask about, and the honest answer is that the easement runs with the land and the arrangement predates both households. Have the deed language ready at the first showing rather than the third.

06  Four roads to the same number

A single method is an opinion. Four that agree is a price.

Each of these was run independently, and two of them were backtested — run against hundreds of Natick sales where the answer was already known, to measure how wrong the method typically is. That error figure is printed next to each one, because a number without an error bar is a guess wearing a suit.

Square footage we market

Why this toggle exists. The town says 1,532. The twin next door was marketed at 1,832 — 1,582 above grade plus 250 below. Counting every finished room including the lower level gets you past 2,000. All four are defensible; they are not equally defensible. 1,832 is the one I would put in the listing, because it is exactly the basis the identical house next door used, and it is the basis the comparable set is measured on.

Method A · Assessment ratio
$917,000
Natick homes sell at a median 1.207× their prior-year assessment. Measured on 64 West Natick sales. Median error 6.7% — the most accurate of the four. This is the median-condition answer: what 24 Bishop is worth presenting like everything else on the market.
Method B · Paired sale
$844,000
The identical twin at 22 Bishop, sold July 2021 at $675,000, carried forward. Strongest possible physical match; weakest link is the five-year index. Range $810,000–$878,000.
Method C · Adjusted grid
$815,000
The six-comparable grid in section 04, reconciled to the two best-calibrated sales — 14 Hardwick Rd (closed sixteen days ago, within 1% of the subject’s size) and 3 Oxbow Rd (the only house in 453 sales to trade twice). This is the method an appraiser will use, so it is the one that has to hold up.
Method D · Price per sq ft
$848,000
$463/sq ft × 1,832 sq ft. West Natick median. Median error 8.7% — the bluntest instrument here, included because every buyer will do this arithmetic on their phone.
Method A sits well above the rest, and that gap is not an error — it is the exterior and the paperwork. But A also assumes a house that presents like every other sale in its assessment class, and this one does not, for a reason no cosmetic work can fix: it sits at the end of a shared drive with no street presence. That thins the buyer pool, and a thin pool is how you lose the competitive bidding that produced the $900,000-plus results in this comp set. The conclusion leans on C, the two best-calibrated sales, and treats A as the ceiling rather than the target.
07  The question you actually asked

Yes — and the walkway before the driveway.

Be clear about what this work does. It does not make the house worth more than the market says it is worth. It removes a discount the house is carrying right now. You are buying back $35,000, not manufacturing it — and the house sells either way. This is a lever on price and market time, not a condition of sale.

Here is the mechanism, because it matters more than the list. A buyer's opinion of this house is formed before they reach the front door. They come down a long shared drive, park on gravel, walk up a mismatched brick path with moss in the joints, past siding with a grime line at the bottom, under a deck whose finish gave out years ago. Then they step inside — granite, stainless, two updated full baths, hardwood everywhere. That does not read as a well-kept home. It reads as a surprise, and a surprise reads as luck rather than as the standard. Every showing starts from a deduction, and every inspection item lands on ground you already prepared for it.

The comparable set prices this openly. Homes described as updated and well-presented traded at $462 to $510 a square foot. The dated one — 143 Howe Street — traded at $350. Your interior already belongs in the first group. Only the outside is voting for the second.

Two tiers, priced as a share of value

We are not contractors — get three quotes. These are planning ranges only.

ScopeWhat it coversShare of valuePlanning range

Tier 2 — add the full walkway Everything above, plus the complete walk: demolition, disposal, a proper frost-depth base, and one material from the drive to the door tying into the pavers already in back ≈ 1.9% $11,100 – $20,900

Tier 1 is the clear yes — under one percent of value, and it kills the two strongest neglect signals on the property. Tier 2 is a preference, not a return. The extra spend on the walkway buys back roughly what it costs; do it if they want the top of the range and have three weeks, not if it means borrowing. And the ordering you gave them holds: the walk is in every approach, every photograph and every showing. The pothole is in none of them.

The paperwork, and why a buyer cares

Three things exist in this house and not in the town's records: the finished upper level, the electric heat in nearly every room, and a second full bath. That is the −$20,000 "permits & records" line running against every comparable in section 04, and it is worth understanding what a buyer is actually pricing there.

  • The appraiser will not count it. Unpermitted finished area does not go into the gross living area on an appraisal, so the upper level supports no value on paper even though a buyer will stand in it and want it.
  • The lender can stall. Some underwriters require open work to be permitted and signed off before they will clear to close. That is a timeline risk on a deal that is otherwise clean.
  • The inspector will find it. Sloped-ceiling finished space and whole-house electric heat are exactly what a home inspector flags. Found in week six by their inspector it is a re-trade; disclosed in week one by you it is a known quantity.
  • It follows them. Whoever buys inherits the same disclosure obligation when they sell. Buyers know that, and they price it.
The single most important fact in this section: the work was done by professional tradesmen, not by the homeowner. The electric heat was installed by a licensed electrician, and the deck it replaced was permitted and inspected in 2007. What is missing is the paperwork, not the workmanship — and those are very different problems with very different price tags. An as-built permit closes a filing gap. There is no evidence of anything needing to be rebuilt.

Which is why item 01 on the pre-listing list is worth doing before the sign goes up. Pulling as-built permits converts an open-ended inspection risk into a closed file, and it moves that −$20,000 line to −$5,000.

And four things not to do

  • Don't repave the driveway. Thousands of dollars on a surface buyers read as shared and semi-rural anyway. Patch the hole and stop.
  • Don't touch the kitchen or the baths. They already test at the top of this comparable set. Money spent there is money donated.
  • Don't replace the siding. It is vinyl, it is sound, and it is dirty. Those are different problems with a $600 difference in price.
  • Don't finish anything else. The unfinished attic stays unfinished — there is one open permit question already and no reason to add a second.
08  Pricing to the search box

The asking price is not the value. It is a filter setting.

Buyers do not browse. They set a maximum and let the portal decide what they ever see. Those maximums are round: seven-fifty, eight hundred, eight-fifty, nine hundred. A house priced at $815,000 is invisible to every buyer who capped their search at $800,000 — and to a buyer searching $800,000 to $850,000 it is just another listing in the middle of the pile. It has managed to be both too expensive and unremarkable at the same time.

Price the same house at $799,000 and it appears in front of the entire under-$800,000 cohort, and shows up as the least expensive thing on the page for everyone whose ceiling is higher. That is not a discount. It is a distribution decision, and in a market where homes are closing at or above asking it costs nothing.

And there is a sharper reason, specific to this house

Think about who each price band actually contains, because the three groups want completely different things.

  • The buyer searching to $800,000. For them this is a stretch — and a stretch worth making. Nearly an acre, three finished levels, two garage bays, a 1996 house when everything else in their range was built in 1950. The deck and the walk are things they will happily take on over a few summers, because the alternative at their number is smaller and older. This house is the best thing they will see.
  • The buyer searching to $850,000. They can comfortably afford it and they can afford to fix it. But at their number they are also looking at houses with nothing to do, so this one reads as a project — affordable, and declined.
  • The buyer searching to $900,000. No interest whatsoever. Wrong size, wrong arrival, wrong street presence. They are not the market for it at any price.
So the buyer who values this house most is the one capped at $800,000 — and at an asking price of $815,000 or $819,000, that buyer never sees it exists. You would be hiding the house from the exact person most likely to fall in love with it, in order to protect a number the market was going to bid past anyway. That is the whole argument for $799,000, and it holds even if the value really is $819,000.

This is not a theory — 42% of Natick already does it

Across 337 Natick single-family asking prices — every active listing plus everything closed in the last twelve months — 42% are priced deliberately just under a $25,000 or $50,000 bracket. Only 24% sit exactly on a round number. Nearly 17% end in the digits 900. Agents in this town are already pricing to the filter; the question is only whether you do it on purpose.

So, for 24 Bishop Street

List as-is
$799,000

Against a value of $815,000. Deliberately beneath the $800,000 wall. You give up nothing — this market bids credible listings up — and you gain the one cohort that wants this house more than anyone else does.

List after the work
$849,000

Against a value of $850,000. One thousand under the $850,000 wall, which is exactly what 28 Barnesdale Road did before closing seventy-five thousand over. Listing at $850,000 flat would be the worst available choice — the same buyers, minus the ones who capped at $850K.

Never price a house on a bracket. $850,000 and $849,000 reach different audiences and cost you the same. The thousand dollars is not a concession — it is the price of admission to a search result.

11  Before we go live

Seven things to nail down, and who nails them down.

None of these change the price. All of them change how smoothly the sale goes, and several of them are the difference between disclosing something on your terms in week one and defending it on a buyer's terms in week six.

  1. Pull as-built permits for the upper level and the electrical
    Natick Building Department. The work was done by a licensed electrician, which is the hard part already solved. An as-built electrical permit plus a building permit for the finished space converts an open-ended inspection risk into a closed file. Budget a few thousand and start now — this is the long-lead item on the list.
    Zev to open · seller
  2. Have the oil system serviced and certified
    This one is a genuine opportunity. If the oil warm-air system runs, the story changes from "electric heat" — which frightens Massachusetts buyers — to "oil heat with independent electric zone control in every room," which is a feature. Get a service company to fire it, tag it and put it in writing.
    Seller · before photos
  3. Confirm town water versus private well
    There is a softener and a sediment filter in the lower level. That is common on Natick town water and also common on a well. The listing has to say which, and it has to be right.
    Seller · one phone call
  4. Get the driveway easement language out of the deed
    Book 26455, Page 361. Have the exact grant, its width and its maintenance terms ready as a listing attachment. The question gets asked at every showing; answering it in writing up front removes it as a negotiating lever.
    Zev · registry pull
  5. Measure the house properly
    Floor plan and measurement by a third party. The town's 1,532 has been wrong since 2003 and the twin's 1,832 is a reasonable but borrowed figure. On a house whose value hinges on square footage that nobody has verified in twenty-three years, a $300 measurement is the cheapest insurance in this document.
    Zev to order
  6. Count the baths on the record
    The card says one full and one half. The house has two full and one half. That gets corrected with the assessor at the same time as the permits, not separately.
    Bundle with item 01
  7. Pull the survey stakes before photography
    Two orange markers are still standing in the gravel apron. They photograph as a boundary dispute whether or not there is one.
    Ten minutes

Why both of those list prices sit at or under the value

Because this comp set is unusually clear about what happens either way, and because of the search-bracket argument in section 08. Ten of twenty comparable sales closed over asking, and the four largest gains all sat just beneath a round number. Then there is 23 Porter Road, two thirds of a mile away, which reached for $899,900 and closed at $820,000 after 62 days. In Natick right now, pricing under the bracket invites competition and pricing past it buys a price cut.

The recommendation, in one line

If you list now, as it stands
$799,000

Reconciled value $815,000. This prices deliberately beneath the $800,000 wall to reach the buyer who wants this house most. Expect $795,000–$835,000 and roughly 45–60 days to an accepted offer — from a buyer who opens the negotiation standing on the deck.

If you spend three weeks and $15,000 first
$849,000

Reconciled value $850,000, priced one thousand under the $850,000 bracket — exactly what 28 Barnesdale Road did before closing seventy-five thousand over. Expect $830,000–$870,000, a shorter market time, and a listing that no longer hands the buyer their opening argument.

My recommendation is the second one — but it is a recommendation, not a requirement. The house sells either way. Roughly two percent of value, spent over about three weeks, recovers a discount of more than four percent and moves this house out of the $350-a-foot pile and into the $462-to-$510 one. That is not a rounding difference. On 1,832 square feet it is the whole conversation. If they would rather list now and take $815,000, that is a completely legitimate choice and we will run it hard.
